title: Uddhava Begs Krishna Not to Leave Him Behind
story:
The omens had begun to appear in Dwaraka, Krishna's city by the sea — small ones at first, a strange bird on a rooftop, a vessel of milk soured before its time — and then signs that made the city speak in low voices. Krishna read them all, and grew quiet.

Uddhava, Krishna's dearest friend, had lately returned from Vrindavan, where he had carried Krishna's own message of comfort to the cowherds; he had brought their longing home with him — Nanda's grief, the cowherd women's tears, the old villagers who had pressed his hand as if they had touched Krishna himself. Now, in Dwaraka, he read the omens for what they were. The work Krishna had come to do was done. Krishna meant to leave the world.

Dwaraka seemed to feel it before anyone said a word. The city had grown rich and proud, and its pride had begun to work like a slow fever: feasts that lasted too long, quarrels that flared over a look, young men of the Yadu clans who had forgotten how to fear anything. The elders whispered that the family had grown too great for the earth to hold it, and the omens seemed to say the same. Only Krishna moved through it all untroubled — speaking gently, settling disputes, smiling at children — and Uddhava, watching him, understood that this calm was itself a kind of farewell.

Uddhava found him alone, fell at his feet, and for a long moment could not speak. At last he said: "Krishna, I cannot bear to leave your feet, even for half a moment. Wherever you go, carry me too, to your own abode."

Then, with Krishna's hand resting on his head, everything he had stored up in silence came out. Krishna's pastimes, he said, were the greatest good fortune a human being could meet; nothing in any of the three worlds stood beside them. The bed Krishna had slept in, the seat he had sat on, the roads he had walked, the river pools where he had bathed, his games and his meals, the garlands that had lain on his chest, the scents he wore, his clothes, his ornaments — Uddhava had kept each of them like a secret treasure, and he could not give up the source of them all. Even the ascetics who renounce everything — who throw away wealth and home and name, and wear only the wind for clothing — wander the world with nothing, remembering Krishna and singing his deeds. They never once touched his hand, and they cannot let him go. If the memory of Krishna keeps a man alive who has given up the whole world, what holds the one who held nothing back — who poured his whole life into that one friendship, and was trusted in return with Krishna's deepest errands?

He said all of it with his face against the ground, and when he had finished he lay still, waiting.

Krishna raised him up with his own hands. "What you have said is exactly my own intent," he said. "Brahma, Shiva, and the gods who guard the worlds are longing for my return to heaven. The time has come." He spoke of their longing simply, without triumph, the way one mentions an old appointment kept at last. And he granted Uddhava his prayer — he would not be left behind.

But that was not all he granted. In the quiet of that hour, with the troubled city beyond the walls, Krishna began to instruct him, as a teacher speaks to a disciple he loves — about the self, the world, and the way to freedom. Uddhava had begged to be carried; he received instead something harder and greater: the teaching that would let him stand, and stand alone, after Krishna had gone.
reflection: Uddhava's plea measures devotion not by what a devotee has done but by how near the beloved is: even the sages who have renounced everything cling to the memory of Krishna's deeds, so how could the man who lived beside him bear a moment's separation? And Krishna's answer transforms the request — he grants Uddhava's wish to be carried along, and then gives him something that makes the wish unnecessary: the teaching that lets him stand alone.
next_story_tease: And he began his teaching with a story — of a king who met a wandering sage on a forest road.
hero_scene: In a quiet room in Dwaraka, Uddhava lies prostrate at Krishna's feet, his face against the ground, while Krishna bends to raise him with both hands and the troubled city waits beyond the walls.
